subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

section_titles: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
periods.activity_title: Hidden Seeds and Sweet Sums on the Tens Frame

tasks_in_class.description: Perform the hidden-seed magic trick with friends; write the number of hidden seeds in the table for six total-and-visible pairs.
Draw the number of dots for 7 balushahi + 5 balushahi and 7 balushahi – 5 balushahi; complete the number sentences.
Card Game: shuffle four sets of number cards 1–10; take turns opening one card; keep any three cards that form an addition or subtraction statement.

time_bands.activity: Children work in pairs to run the hidden-seed trick from Let us Do, p.29 ("perform the hidden-seed magic trick...hidden seeds in the table"). One child hides a handful of seeds under a cloth; the partner uses the total and the visible count to name the hidden amount. Pairs rotate roles and fill in all six rows of the table.

Introduce the tens frame using Let us Do, p.30 ("draw dots for 7 balushahi + 5 balushahi and 7 – 5..."). Children draw dots in the frame for both expressions side by side, then write the matching number sentences. The teacher draws attention to how the same three numbers appear in both sentences.

Children play the Card Game from Let us Play, p.31 ("shuffle four sets of number cards 1–10; keep three cards forming addition or subtraction"). Groups of three take turns flipping cards; any player who assembles a valid statement claims the trio. After play, each group shares one statement they collected.

periods.teacher_notes: The hidden-seed trick anchors subtraction as a missing-addend problem — children feel the question before they see the symbol. When recording tens-frame dot patterns, watch for children who draw dots without counting — prompt them to touch each dot as they place it. The card game surfaces the same add/subtract relationship playfully; accept any valid statement a child can read aloud correctly.
materials: Seeds or pebbles (a small handful per pair)
A handkerchief or piece of cloth per pair
Tens-frame printed sheets or drawn grids
Four sets of number cards 1–10 per group

section_titles: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
periods.activity_title: Tens Frame to Ginladi — Bridging to 100

tasks_in_class.description: Use the tens frame to solve: (a) 6+8 (b) 5+10 (c) 9–6 (d) 18–9.
Nandini and Chirag have 22 stamps; Nani Maa's brother gives 30 more — find the total using the ginladi.
52 stamps total, 37 with famous persons — find how many show monuments (52 – 37); find other ways on the number line.

time_bands.activity: Children complete the four tens-frame calculations from Let us Do, p.31 ("solve 6+8, 5+10, 9–6, 18–9 using the tens frame"). They draw dot patterns and write the number sentence beside each. Two or three children share their drawings on the board.

Introduce the ginladi (bead string) using Let us Do, p.32 ("22 stamps plus 30 more — find the total using the ginladi"). The teacher demonstrates counting on from 22 in jumps of 10, then invites children to try the same on individual bead strings or drawn number lines. Children record the jump path and the answer.

Children work on Let us Do, p.33 ("52 stamps, 37 with famous persons — find how many show monuments"). They try at least two different jump paths for 52 – 37 and write the number sentence for each. Volunteers describe their chosen path aloud, emphasising that different routes reach the same answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The tens-frame work builds on the dot-drawing children did with the balushahi context; connect the two explicitly by asking 'What tool helps us see the total quickly?' as you move to the ginladi. The most common error when subtracting on the bead string is counting the starting bead as jump one — model starting from the bead and jumping past it. Celebrate children who find a second route for 52 – 37.
materials: Tens-frame printed sheets
Bead strings or printed 1–100 number lines (one per child)
Coloured pencils or crayons for marking jumps

section_titles: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
periods.activity_title: Missing Stamps and Jump Strategies on the Ginladi

tasks_in_class.description: They have 52 stamps and want 75 — figure out how many more stamps they need using the number line.
Solve using a ginladi: (a) 34+6 (b) 23+12 (c) 33–5 (d) 42–15.
A frog is at 7 and jumps 10 beads at a time — mark the beads it will land on and write the numbers.
The grasshopper at 76 jumps backward by 10 each time — mark all beads it will jump on and write the numbers.

homework.description: Fill in the jump tables by jumping as instructed for Jump 5, Jump 6, and Jump 9 from given starting numbers.

time_bands.activity: Children tackle Let us Do, p.33 ("52 stamps and want 75 — how many more stamps are needed?"). They mark 52 on the number line and jump forward to 75, recording the total jump. Pairs compare their routes and confirm they reach the same answer.

Children work through Let us Do Q1, p.34 ("solve 34+6, 23+12, 33–5, 42–15 using the ginladi"). Each calculation gets its own number-line strip; children draw the jumps in coloured pencil and write the answer at the landing point.

The class acts out the frog from Let us Do Q2, p.34 ("frog at 7 jumps 10 at a time — mark landing beads"). Children mark the sequence on their number lines, then write the landing numbers. Without pausing, move to Let us Do Q4, p.34 ("grasshopper at 76 jumps backward by 10") — children mark the descending sequence and write the numbers.

A quick class discussion: 'What do you notice about the numbers the frog lands on? What about the grasshopper?' Children share observations about the tens digit changing while the ones digit stays the same. The jump tables in Let us Do Q5, p.35 are set as an unhurried take-home task.

periods.teacher_notes: Knowing the stamp count so far (52) and the target (75) frames subtraction as a missing-addend problem — the same idea met earlier with hidden seeds. Watch for children who jump past 75 and cannot account for the overshoot; guide them to make tens-jumps and then smaller ones to land exactly. The frog and grasshopper patterns reveal that adding or subtracting 10 changes only the tens digit — let children state this in their own words before you confirm it.
materials: Bead strings or printed 1–100 number lines (one per child)
Coloured pencils or crayons
Printed or drawn 100-bead ginladi for teacher demonstration

section_titles: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100

tasks_in_class.description: The frog again jumps forward by 10 from 23 — mark all landing places on the ginladi.
Fill in the jump tables by jumping as instructed for Jump 5, Jump 6, and Jump 9 from given starting numbers.

time_bands.activity: Children mark the frog's path from Let us Do Q3, p.34 ("frog jumps forward by 10 from 23 — mark all landing places"). They list the landing numbers and compare with the sequence from 7 (Q2) to notice the ones digit is always 3 here, always 7 there. The teacher invites children to predict the fifth and sixth landing numbers before marking them.

Children fill the jump tables in Let us Do Q5, p.35 ("Jump 5, Jump 6, Jump 9 from given starting numbers"). They work independently, marking each jump on the number line first, then transferring the landing value to the table. After completing Jump 5, the class pauses to check together; children describe the pattern they see in the ones digits before continuing with Jump 6 and Jump 9.

A closing sharing: pairs read out one row of their Jump 9 table. The teacher asks 'Does everyone have the same numbers?' and draws out that the sequence is the same regardless of who filled it — reinforcing that jump tables follow a fixed additive pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who completed the Jump 5 table as a take-home task can cross-check with peers at the start — but the unit is designed so that all three jump tables are completed in class. The Jump 9 table is the most demanding; encourage children to use the number line rather than mental recall, and to check by counting back. Watch for confusion between 'jumping 9' and 'landing on a multiple of 9' — the starting number matters.
materials: Printed 1–100 number lines (one per child)
Coloured pencils (two colours)
Jump-table worksheet or textbook p.35

section_titles: Addition and subtraction on the 100-number grid
periods.activity_title: Moving on the 100 Grid — Dice Game and Arrow Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Number Grid Game: players roll two dice to form a two-digit number and move a counter forward or backward on the 100 grid; first to reach 91–100 wins.
Use the number grid to find where each player lands: (a) 45+34 (b) 75+56 (c) 30+66 (d) 89+63; show thinking by drawing arrows in the grid.

time_bands.activity: The teacher projects or draws a 100-number grid and walks children through how movement works: one step right adds 1, one step down adds 10. Children practise by calling out where a counter lands after given moves — for example, starting at 34, moving right 3 and down 2.

Pairs play the Number Grid Game from Let us Play, p.35 ("roll two dice to form a two-digit number; move counter forward or backward; first to 91–100 wins"). Each player records the two-digit number formed, the starting square, and the landing square after each turn.

Children use the number grid to solve Let us Do Q1(a–d), p.36 ("find landing squares for 45+34, 75+56, 30+66, 89+63; draw arrows"). They draw right-arrows for ones and down-arrows for tens directly on a printed grid. Pairs share how they handled sums that went beyond 100.

periods.teacher_notes: The number grid encodes place-value structure in two directions — emphasise this when a counter moves down a row ('we added a ten; which digit changed?'). When sums exceed 100 in Q1(b) and Q1(d), let children discover the counter runs off the grid and discuss what that means for the answer. The dice game is a fast, open-ended way to build familiarity with the grid before the structured arrow problems.
materials: Printed 100-number grids (at least two per child — one for the game, one for Q1)
Counters or coins (two per pair)
Two standard dice per pair
Coloured pencils for arrows

section_titles: Magic Sums — row and column addition puzzles
periods.activity_title: Magic Sums — Rows, Columns and Diagonals

tasks_in_class.description: Observe the completed Magic Sums puzzle; fill three incomplete grids so each row and column adds to the given target; add blue-box and red-box numbers and describe what you find.
Fill the blanks to complete the magic square (3×3 grid with 3, 9, and 6 given).

time_bands.activity: Children examine the completed Magic Sums example on p.37. The teacher asks: 'Check each row — what do you get? Check each column.' Children add aloud. Then: 'Now add the blue-box numbers. Now the red-box numbers. What do you notice?' Children share observations in their own words.

Children fill the three incomplete grids from Magic Sums, p.37 ("fill so each row and column adds to the given target; describe blue-box and red-box totals"). They work individually, checking rows and columns as they go. After finishing, they add the diagonal boxes and record what they find.

Children attempt the magic square in Magic Sums, p.37 ("complete the 3×3 grid given 3, 9, and 6"). They may use trial and adjust — trying a number, checking the row and column sums, swapping if needed. The teacher circulates and asks 'How do you know that number belongs there?'

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight children should reach independently is that the diagonal totals equal the row and column totals — state it only after they have described it themselves. The most common error is repeating a digit; remind children that each digit 1–9 appears exactly once. The magic square with 3, 9, and 6 given is genuinely harder — celebrate partial progress and encourage a fresh attempt rather than giving the answer.
materials: Textbook p.37 (Magic Sums)
Pencils and erasers (trial-and-adjust work requires erasing)

section_titles: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
periods.activity_title: Radish Fields — Estimating, Box Diagrams and Number Lines

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate total radishes; draw the 25+36 problem as a box diagram; find the answer using matchstick bundles or the number line; find other ways on the number line.
Estimate the number of carrots in a box of 100 (with 65 tomatoes); circle the bundle of sticks showing the correct count; solve 100–65 on the number line.
Draw a box diagram for 85+67 apples; estimate whether the total is more or less than 100 and explain your reasoning.

time_bands.activity: Children open at Let us Do, p.38 ("estimate total radishes; draw 25+36 as a box diagram; find the answer"). They first write an estimate, then draw the box diagram with 25 and 36 as the two parts. Using matchstick bundles (tens as a bundle of ten sticks, ones as singles), they group and regroup to find the total, then verify with a number-line jump.

Children work on p.39 ("estimate carrots in a box of 100 with 65 tomatoes; circle the correct bundle; solve 100–65 on the number line"). They write an estimate before circling, then mark the jump from 65 to 100 on the number line and record the difference.

Children draw a box diagram for the apple problem on p.40 ("draw box diagram for 85+67; estimate and explain whether more or less than 100"). They write their estimate with a reason ('I think more than 100 because 85 is already close to 100 and we add 67 more'). The teacher listens to two or three explanations and asks 'How did you decide?'

periods.teacher_notes: Estimation is the cognitive priority in this unit — ask children to commit to an estimate before they touch the bundles or number line, so the subsequent calculation has something to check against. When drawing box diagrams, some children draw the two parts without labelling them; insist on writing the number inside each box. The carrot problem (100 – 65) is the first subtraction from 100 children encounter in this context — use the complement idea from the hidden-seed work if children are stuck.
materials: Matchsticks or craft sticks (at least 120 per group of four)
Rubber bands or string for bundling
Printed number lines extending to at least 160
Pencils and rulers for box diagrams

section_titles: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
periods.activity_title: Apple Harvest — Solving Beyond 100 and Word Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Find 85+67 using the number line; find who collected more apples and by how much (85–67).
Q1–Q5: Solve word problems (books sold, cricket runs, vadas, dried plants) by drawing box diagrams and using matchstick bundles or number line; make and share your own word problem.

time_bands.activity: Children calculate 85+67 from p.41 ("find 85+67 using the number line") by marking jumps of tens and ones from 85. They then tackle 85–67 ("who collected more apples and by how much") using the same number line, jumping from 67 up to 85 and reading the gap. Pairs compare their jump strategies.

Children work through the word problems Q1–Q5 on p.42 ("solve books sold, cricket runs, vadas, dried plants problems; draw box diagrams"). For each problem they: write an estimate, draw the box diagram, choose a representation (matchstick bundles or number line), and write the answer. After Q4, children compose their own word problem and swap with a neighbour to solve.

Two or three children read their invented word problems aloud. The class decides which operation is needed and gives a quick estimate. The teacher connects back: 'We used addition when two groups join, subtraction when we compare or find what is left over — just like with the radishes and the stamps.'

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse whether to add or subtract in comparison problems ('who collected more') — the box diagram with the two parts and the total labelled helps them see the structure before choosing the operation. When children compose their own word problems, accept informal language but ask them to name the two quantities and what is being found. The connection drawn at the close between the harvest context and the stamp context reinforces that addition and subtraction are the same operations regardless of setting.
materials: Printed number lines extending to at least 160
Matchsticks or craft sticks
Pencils and rulers for box diagrams
Textbook pp.41–42

section_titles: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100

tasks_in_class.description: Two-player game: alternate adding a number between 1 and 10 to a running total; first player to reach exactly 100 wins.
Q1: Estimate each expression and match it to 'more than 100' or 'less than 100'. Q2: Solve all the expressions using a number line and write the answers.

time_bands.activity: Pairs play the Race to 100 game from Let us Play, p.42 ("alternate adding 1–10 to a running total; first to reach exactly 100 wins"). Each player keeps a running written record of the total after each turn. After two rounds the teacher asks: 'Did you find a strategy to control where you land? Which numbers did you try to reach first?'

Children complete Q1 of Let us Do Q1–2, p.43 ("estimate each expression; match to more than 100 or less than 100"). They write their reasoning in a phrase ('45+62 — both are near 50, so the total is near 100 or more') before drawing the matching arrow.

Children solve all expressions in Q2 of Let us Do Q1–2, p.43 ("solve on the number line and write the answers") and check whether each answer matches their earlier estimate. The teacher asks: 'Was your estimate right? If not, what did you miss?' Children share one expression where their estimate matched and one where it did not.

periods.teacher_notes: The Race to 100 game, played after the word-problem and box-diagram work, shifts children from following a given procedure to choosing their own numbers strategically — this is the chapter's richest reasoning moment. Watch for children who recognise that reaching 90 with their turn gives them control of the endgame; name this as 'thinking ahead about what the other player can do'. The estimation-then-compute structure in Q1–Q2 closes the chapter by making the link between approximate reasoning and exact calculation explicit.
materials: Pencils and paper for recording running totals (Race to 100)
Printed number lines extending to at least 160
Textbook p.43

items.prompt: There are 9 seeds in all. You can see 4 seeds on the table. How many seeds are hiding under the cloth? Show your thinking.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start with the total (9), count back the visible seeds (4) to find the hidden amount: 9 – 4 = 5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use pebbles on the desk and cover some; stretch: ask them to write two different totals where 5 seeds could be hidden.

exercise.description: Perform the hidden-seed magic trick with friends; write the number of hidden seeds in the table for six total-and-visible pairs.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
items.prompt: Draw dots in a tens frame to show 8 + 4. Then draw dots in another tens frame to show 8 – 4. Write the number sentence for each.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Tens frame for 8+4: 10 filled and 2 more = 12. Number sentence: 8 + 4 = 12. Tens frame for 8–4: 8 dots, remove 4, leaving 4. Number sentence: 8 – 4 = 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fill the tens frame dot by dot and count the total or remaining dots to read the answer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a printed tens frame and counters to place physically; stretch: ask the child to write a third sentence using the same three numbers in a different order.

exercise.description: Draw the number of dots for 7 balushahi + 5 balushahi and 7 balushahi – 5 balushahi; complete the number sentences.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: Draw a box diagram for this problem: Riya has 34 mangoes and her friend has 48 mangoes. Before you calculate, estimate — do you think the total is more than 100 or less than 100? Write one sentence explaining your estimate.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The box diagram has two parts labelled 34 and 48 and a total box on top. The total is more than 100 because 34 + 48: 30 + 40 = 70 and 4 + 8 = 12, so 70 + 12 = 82 — wait, 82 is less than 100. Correct answer: the total is less than 100 (82). A valid estimate explanation: '34 is about 35 and 48 is about 50; 35 + 50 = 85, which is less than 100.'
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw the two parts in the box diagram, estimate by rounding each to the nearest ten, then compare the rounded sum to 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to round each number to the nearest ten first and add those rounded numbers; stretch: ask them to now find the exact total using a number line.

exercise.description: Estimate total radishes; draw the 25+36 problem as a box diagram; find the answer using matchstick bundles or the number line; find other ways on the number line.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A basket has 100 oranges. 72 are taken out. Without calculating exactly, which is the best estimate for the number of oranges left?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that 72 is close to 70; 100 – 70 = 30, so the remainder is near 30.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have halved 100 rather than subtracting 72, confusing 'half' with 'take away'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have subtracted a much smaller number (about 10–20) instead of 72, possibly misreading the problem.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have added 72 to 100 rather than subtracting, reversing the operation.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to mark 100 and 72 on a number line and find the gap; stretch: ask them to find the exact answer and check whether it falls in their chosen range.

exercise.description: Draw a box diagram for 85+67 apples; estimate whether the total is more or less than 100 and explain your reasoning.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
items.prompt: Priya picks three number cards: 6, 9, and 3. Can she make an addition statement and a subtraction statement using all three cards? Write both statements.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Addition: 6 + 3 = 9. Subtraction: 9 – 3 = 6 (or 9 – 6 = 3). Both use the same three numbers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the largest number as the total and the other two as parts; write both the addition and the corresponding subtraction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child physical cards and let them arrange and rearrange before writing; stretch: ask them to find a second subtraction statement using the same three numbers.

exercise.description: Card Game: shuffle four sets of number cards 1–10; take turns opening one card; keep any three cards that form an addition or subtraction statement.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A rabbit starts at 4 on the number line and jumps forward 10 beads at a time. Write all the numbers it will land on before it passes 60.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 14, 24, 34, 44, 54. (The rabbit lands at 64 next, which is past 60, so it stops at 54.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 10 repeatedly starting from 4: 4 → 14 → 24 → 34 → 44 → 54; the next jump (64) passes 60, so stop.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark each jump on a printed number line using a pencil; stretch: ask them to write the sequence if the rabbit jumped backward by 10 from 64.

exercise.description: A frog is at 7 and jumps 10 beads at a time — mark the beads it will land on and write the numbers.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A grasshopper is at 85 and jumps backward by 10 each time. Which list shows the numbers it will land on for its first four jumps?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 10 from each landing number in turn: 85 – 10 = 75, 75 – 10 = 65, 65 – 10 = 55, 55 – 10 = 45.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child subtracted 1 each time instead of 10, confusing a jump of 10 beads with a single step.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child added 10 each time instead of subtracting, reversing the direction of the jump.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child subtracted a decreasing number (9, 9, 9…) or applied an inconsistent rule, showing the ones digit is not fixed.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to mark 85 on a number line and physically count back 10 for the first jump; stretch: ask them to predict where the grasshopper will be after 7 jumps.

exercise.description: The grasshopper at 76 jumps backward by 10 each time — mark all beads it will jump on and write the numbers.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the 100-number grid
items.prompt: On a 100-number grid, a counter starts at 23. It moves 4 steps to the right and then 3 steps down. What number does it land on? Explain what the right steps and the down steps each do to the number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The counter lands on 57. Moving right 4 steps adds 4 ones (23 + 4 = 27). Moving down 3 steps adds 3 tens (27 + 30 = 57). Right steps change the ones digit; down steps change the tens digit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the ones (right steps) first, then add the tens (down steps): 23 + 4 = 27, then 27 + 30 = 57.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a printed 100 grid and a counter to move physically; stretch: ask them to find a different path (e.g. down first, then right) and check they reach the same answer.

exercise.description: Number Grid Game: players roll two dice to form a two-digit number and move a counter forward or backward on the 100 grid; first to reach 91–100 wins.

items.section_title: Magic Sums — row and column addition puzzles
items.prompt:
Look at this partly filled grid. Each row and each column must add up to 15. Fill in the two missing numbers.

| 6 | 1 | _ |
| _ | 5 | 4 |
| 3 | 9 | 3 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: 6 + 1 + ? = 15, so ? = 8. Row 2: ? + 5 + 4 = 15, so ? = 6. Check column 1: 6 + 6 + 3 = 15. Check column 3: 8 + 4 + 3 = 15. Both check out.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the known numbers in the row to find the target sum needed, then subtract from 15 to get the missing number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to add each completed row first to confirm the target is 15, then work on one missing cell at a time; stretch: ask them to check both diagonals and say whether they also add to 15.

exercise.description: Observe the completed Magic Sums puzzle; fill three incomplete grids so each row and column adds to the given target; add blue-box and red-box numbers and describe what you find.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: Without calculating, which of these expressions gives a total of more than 100?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each addend to the nearest ten: 50 + 60 = 110, which exceeds 100; the others round to sums below 100.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have picked the largest single number rather than estimating the sum; 74 + 22 = 96.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may have added the tens digits only (50 + 30 = 80) and ignored the ones, missing that the ones push the total past 100.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have rounded carelessly or added incorrectly; 61 + 31 = 92.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to round each number to the nearest 10 and add the rounded numbers first; stretch: ask them to identify which of the remaining expressions comes closest to 100 and by how much.

exercise.description: Q1: Estimate each expression and match it to 'more than 100' or 'less than 100'. Q2: Solve all the expressions using a number line and write the answers.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A box has 100 plums. 58 are taken out and given away. How many are left? Show your working on a number line.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 42 plums are left. On the number line jump from 58 to 60 (+2), then from 60 to 100 (+40): total jump = 2 + 40 = 42.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 58 to the nearest ten (60), then from 60 to 100; add the two jumps: 2 + 40 = 42.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 58 and 100 on the number line for the child and ask them to find the gap using one or two jumps; stretch: ask them to find a second jump route (e.g. one jump of 42) and confirm it gives the same answer.

exercise.description: Estimate the number of carrots in a box of 100 (with 65 tomatoes); circle the bundle of sticks showing the correct count; solve 100–65 on the number line.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
items.prompt: Use the tens frame to solve: 7 + 6 = ?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fill 7 dots in the tens frame, then add 3 more to reach 10, leaving 3 ones: 10 + 3 = 13.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have counted on only 4 instead of 6, losing track mid-count.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have counted 7 as the first count (counting the start number as 1), adding an extra.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may have added 5 instead of 6, stopping one short.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a tens frame to fill with counters; stretch: ask them to write the corresponding subtraction fact using the same three numbers.

exercise.description: Use the tens frame to solve: (a) 6+8 (b) 5+10 (c) 9–6 (d) 18–9.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: Use the number line to solve: 46 + 13 = ?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump 10 forward from 46 to reach 56, then jump 3 more to reach 59.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child jumped 10 then 1, adding only 11 instead of 13.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child jumped 10 then 4, adding 14 instead of 13 — overcounted the ones.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child added only the ones digit (3) and forgot the tens jump of 10.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the two jumps (tens then ones) on a number line for the child and ask them to label the landing spots; stretch: ask them to find a different jump route that reaches the same answer.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A cricket jumps from 15, always moving forward in steps of 6. Fill in the next five numbers where it lands.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 6 to each landing number in turn: 15+6=21, 21+6=27, 27+6=33, 33+6=39, 39+6=45.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to mark 15 on the number line and make one jump of 6, counting on from 15; stretch: ask them to predict where the cricket will land after 10 jumps total.

exercise.description: Fill in the jump tables by jumping as instructed for Jump 5, Jump 6, and Jump 9 from given starting numbers.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: Arjun has 35 stickers. His sister gives him 28 more. How many stickers does Arjun have now? Use the number line to find your answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump 20 forward from 35 to reach 55, then jump 8 more to reach 63.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: suggest the child first jump by tens (35 → 55) and then by ones (55 → 63), marking each landing; stretch: ask them to find the answer by a second route (e.g. jump 5 to reach 40, then jump 23 more).

exercise.description: Nandini and Chirag have 22 stamps; Nani Maa's brother gives 30 more — find the total using the ginladi.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A library has 60 books. It wants to collect 84 books in all. How many more books does it need? Use the number line to find your answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 60 to 80 (+20) then from 80 to 84 (+4): total = 24.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark both 60 and 84 on the number line and ask the child to count the gap in one big jump; stretch: ask them to find two different jump routes and confirm both give 24.

exercise.description: They have 52 stamps and want 75 — figure out how many more stamps they need using the number line.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the 100-number grid
items.prompt: A player's counter is on 32. She rolls the dice and forms the number 45. She moves her counter forward 45 squares on the 100-number grid. What number does she land on?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Move 4 rows down from 32 (adding 40) to reach 72, then move 5 steps right (adding 5) to reach 77.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a printed 100 grid and ask them to move the counter step by step — down for tens, right for ones; stretch: ask what happens if she moves backward 45 squares from 32 instead.

exercise.description: Use the number grid to find where each player lands: (a) 45+34 (b) 75+56 (c) 30+66 (d) 89+63; show thinking by drawing arrows in the grid.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A gardener picked 76 tomatoes in the morning and 48 tomatoes in the evening. How many tomatoes did she pick in all? Draw a box diagram and use a number line to find the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 124 tomatoes. Box diagram: two parts (76 and 48) with total on top. Number line: 76 + 24 = 100, then 100 + 24 = 124.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 76 to 100 (+24), then from 100 to 124 (+24): total = 76 + 48 = 124.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to first jump from 76 to the nearest hundred (100) and record that jump, then jump the remaining amount; stretch: ask them to check their answer by computing 48 + 76 and confirming it gives the same total.

exercise.description: Find 85+67 using the number line; find who collected more apples and by how much (85–67).

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A shop had 115 biscuits. It sold 68 biscuits in the morning. How many biscuits were left? Draw a box diagram and show your working on a number line.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 47 biscuits were left. Box diagram: total 115, one part 68, missing part is the answer. Number line: jump from 68 to 70 (+2), 70 to 115 (+45): 2 + 45 = 47.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 68 to the nearest ten (70), then from 70 to 115; add the two jumps: 2 + 45 = 47.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the box diagram for the child with 115 and 68 labelled, and ask them to use the number line to find the gap; stretch: ask them to verify by checking 68 + 47 = 115.

exercise.description: Q1–Q5: Solve word problems (books sold, cricket runs, vadas, dried plants) by drawing box diagrams and using matchstick bundles or number line; make and share your own word problem.
